chunk_text:
Natural Language Processing, or NLP, is about how we reason about the linguistic perspective. This is the backbone of the latest advancements and applications we see today. NLP has existed for a long time. I have been doing NLP since 2016, but I believe even before that, NLP has existed. Of course, along the way, due to algorithms and hardware advancements, these translate into different applications. But this has already been done very long ago using traditional machine learning. You can see email filtering, summarization, translation (like Google Translate), and sentiment analysis all involve using NLP. Given a text or paragraph, you can determine if the sentiment is positive or not. All of these can be done using traditional machine learning. The application layer has evolved and become more powerful, but the foundations have been done in the past. These are used in different areas, such as search engine queries, where you type words and retrieve documentation, and chatbots. Summarization of documents are some basic applications of using text data.

Keywords: natural language processing, nlp history, traditional machine learning, email filtering, document summarization, language translation, sentiment analysis, search engines, chatbots

Questions this chunk answers:
- What is Natural Language Processing?
- How long has NLP been around?
- What are some early applications of NLP using traditional machine learning?
- Can traditional machine learning be used for sentiment analysis?

chunk_text:
The transformation of text data in terms of application started with statistical models, then RNN and LSTM. We will talk about these on Thursday. These are neural network architectures, specifically recurrent neural networks and long short-term memory. These are outdated today because of Transformers, but it is still applicable to know them. You will see why such specific architectures made sense for text data, similar to computer vision. Then you have language modeling and word embeddings, which are state-of-the-art for embeddings, powering things like Google Translate. Word2Vec is also somewhat outdated now. Encoder-decoder is a very generic term, but historically, people associated it with sequence-to-sequence models, usually for translation tasks. From a neural network perspective, encoding is projecting input data to a high dimension, and decoding is taking this high representation output and using it for a specific task. That is the typical term for encoder-decoder. Attention came out a long time ago, but the first model that gained popularity was BERT, around early 2017. Today we have pre-trained models, and a couple of years back, GPT 3.5 was the first one that got a big boom, but it has existed for quite some time. Pre-GPT 3.5, GPT3, GPT 2.5 were open source. All these miracles actually came from NLP.

Keywords: language model evolution, statistical models, rnn, lstm, transformer, bert, gpt, word2vec, encoder-decoder, sequence-to-sequence, neural networks, attention, pre-trained models

chunk_text:
NLP is the application of using text data, which is unstructured data. From a computer perspective, it does not understand language like humans. Historically, people have always been thinking about how to reason about this text data from a computer perspective. You saw that even for images, there are traditional computer vision techniques to break down the image. All this translated to things like text classification, where people did a lot of feature engineering in the past and put it into traditional machine learning models. Machine translation, using sequence-to-sequence and deep learning LSTM models, was very good, powering Google Translate. Sentiment analysis is very common; it is a classification task where, given a text or sentence, you predict whether it is positive or negative sentiment. Chatbots, while completely changed by large language models today, were complex applications in the past. Siri and Alexa existed long before large language models. People broke it down into understanding the intent, because when you are communicating, there is an intent behind the words. So people thought about predicting the intent of a sentence. There is also summarization, information extraction, topic modeling, speech recognition, and Q&A. NLP is the most talked about application now because of large language models.

Keywords: nlp applications, unstructured text data, text classification, machine translation, sentiment analysis, chatbots, siri, alexa, intent prediction, summarization, information extraction

Questions this chunk answers:
- How do computers process unstructured text data?
- What are some traditional NLP applications?
- How did chatbots like Siri and Alexa work before large language models?
- What is the goal of sentiment analysis?

chunk_text:
For very basic NLP algorithms, we do not talk about semantics. The idea about text data is that it is not always just looking at keywords. For example, when you talk about healthy foods, organic carrots and kale have nothing to do with 'healthy food' from a direct keyword match. What this illustrates is that for some old-school algorithms, many looked at the matching of the text. If there is something 'health', you look for a match with 'healthy', 'health', 'healthcare', or 'food', you look for anything with the word 'food'. But is it generally true that text matching is the only important way to identify similar words? Must the sentence and characters be the same? Not really. What you want to think about is what we call semantics. There is a meaning behind a word, and semantically, it means the same. For example, if you think about fast food, you would associate it with things like Burger King and McDonald's, but from a keyword perspective, they are not exactly matching. Before I go on, I want to ask you from an intuition standpoint: do you think keyword matching is useless? If we are saying that semantics is very important, and we want to understand the deeper, hidden meaning, does that mean exact keyword matching is useless? Is this statement true? I see a lot of people saying no. Why? I want to get some intuition. Why do you feel that keyword matching is important? Why can't I just do semantics for all?

Keywords: semantics, keyword matching, lexical search, semantic search, text similarity, meaning in text, nlp algorithms, healthy foods example

Questions this chunk answers:
- What is the difference between semantics and keyword matching?
- Why is keyword matching not always sufficient for understanding text?
- Is exact keyword matching still useful in NLP?
- How do older NLP algorithms approach text understanding?
